newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Mobutu's military band marches to a new tune.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's military band marches to a new tune.

text.p: Trumpeting the praises of Mobutu Sese Seko is over for his brass band. On Thursday it was pressed into service by Laurent Kabila for his swearing-in as president of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The 250-strong band provided the musical backing as Kabila took his oath of office in Kinshasa's huge, Chinese-built stadium after a seven-month war to oust Mobutu, who had dominated the former Zaire for over three decades.

"After Kabila took over they came to us and asked us to play for them, and we said yes because we are a military band and we follow orders," bandmaster Major Kawamonoko Ngodia told Reuters. "We played for Mobutu when he was president and now we will play for Kabila."
So far the only new tune the band has had to learn is the Congolese national anthem, which Mobutu changed in the early 1970s when he rebaptised the former Belgian colony and called it Zaire.
"Mostly we play military tunes and they don't change from one government to the next," said Kawamonoko.

When chants of protest erupted from the crowd at Kabila's swearing-in, the band, actually the combined bands of three military forces, was called on to turn up the volume with one of its more rousing numbers to drown out the protestors.
The most obvious change for the bandsmen has been their footwear.

All are now equipped with the wellington boots that the rebels used for their march across Congo -- and which won a major role in African warfare on the feet of Rwandan and Ugandan armies who are Kabila's closest allies.
"We don't really like the new boots, we like real boots, but these are only temporary and soon we will get proper boots with laces again," said tuba player Mukena Kanonge.

Instruments are kept highly polished and musical discipline is faultless -- in marked contrast to the behaviour of Mobutu's ragged army, which fled before Kabila's rebels leaving a trail of pillage and destruction.
Although they were given some training in the use of arms, the band never fought in the civil war.
Bandsmen said the last time they had played for Mobutu was when he returned to Kinshasa in December after cancer surgery in Europe, and promised to defeat Kabila's rebels.
"We always tried to do a good job for Mobutu and we hope that under this government we will be paid a more decent living for our music," said percussionist Kayumba Mukingo.

Protestors in Kinshasa accuse Kabila of using troops from neighbouring Rwanda and Uganda to spearhead his war, but instrumentalists insist that there are no tensions over nationality in the musical section.
"I can assure you that we are all Congolese, there are no Rwandans or Ugandans in the band," said Kayumba.
The bandsmen were not the only group in the stadium to be marching to a different tune now Mobutu has gone.

A group of women, who until two weeks ago called themselves 'Mobutu's Mamas' and wore cotton print dresses emblazoned with his face, came with placards and banners proclaiming Kabila's virtues and calling on people to support him.

"We always support the papa whoever that is. We used to support Mobutu, now we support Kabila. If he goes we will support whoever comes," said Mama Ikali Marie, leader of the newly renamed 'Mothers of the Alliance'.
